rationale: The 8 ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner and protocol, so much of the variance in the raw connectivity features is just site. I z-score each feature within each site, using that site's own subjects (train and test pooled, no labels used). The ADHD/control ratio also differs by site, so I add site one-hot columns scaled ×30. That scaling makes the strong L2 penalty negligible on them, so the model still learns each site's base rate while the connectivity weights come from within-site differences.

rationale: Last round's idea crashed only because `site` arrived as an Arrow-backed pandas column, which can't be indexed with `[:, None]`. This version keeps the same idea. Each connectivity feature is z-scored within its scanner site, using that site's train and test subjects together (no labels involved). Site one-hot columns are added and scaled up so the strong L2 penalty barely affects them, which lets the model learn each site's ADHD rate. Site values are now converted to plain numpy strings, and missing site info no longer causes a crash.

ADHD is diagnosed about 2–3 times more often in boys than girls, and ADHD-200 recruited a mixed age range across sites. Sex and age are therefore strong label-free priors. I add them as scaled-up covariate columns, so the strong L2 penalty barely affects them, in the same way as the site one-hots. The connectivity weights still come from within-site variation.

I'm switching the connectivity measure from Fisher-z Pearson correlations to a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrices. In a published benchmark (Dadi et al. 2019, on ABIDE and ADHD-200), this was the most accurate connectivity measure. The shrinkage also keeps estimates stable for short-scan sites where timepoints are fewer than the 200 ROIs, and for ROIs that are all zero. The reference point is the label-free log-Euclidean mean over all subjects. Everything downstream stays the same: per-site standardization, the scaled covariates and the L2 logistic regression.

Different parcellations each have their own noise and boundary errors, and published fMRI classification benchmarks find that ensembles across atlases are more robust. This change builds the same Ledoit-Wolf tangent-space features on three atlases: CC200 (built from functional data) plus AAL and Harvard-Oxford (anatomical). It fits the same site-standardized, covariate-augmented L2 logistic model on each atlas separately and averages their decision scores. Each atlas's feature-block size is stored in the first columns of the feature matrix, so `fit_predict` can split the blocks apart reliably.

Averaging three atlases gave a clear gain (+0.013), which suggests each parcellation's boundary errors are partly independent. This change adds the other three ADHD-200 parcellations: CC400, a finer functional atlas, and the EZ and TT anatomical atlases. Each new atlas gets the same tangent-space model, and the ensemble averages all six. The extra models should reduce variance further in this low-signal setting with far more features than subjects.

The covariate columns (site, sex, age) are scaled ×30, so the L2 penalty barely touches them. That makes C the setting that decides how much the connectivity weights count against those covariates, and so far C=0.001 has never been tuned. This change picks C (shared across the three atlases) per training fold by grouped inner CV, scoring each candidate on the AUROC of the averaged ensemble score.

I'm adding a fourth model to the ensemble that uses per-ROI time-series features instead of connectivity. The features are pooled across CC200, AAL and HO: log signal SD as an amplitude/ALFF proxy, plus lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelation as proxies for how dominant the low frequencies are. Altered ALFF in ADHD is well documented (e.g. Zang 2007), so this block should carry information the covariance-based models don't. TR differs by site, which would bias the autocorrelation features, but the existing per-site standardization removes that offset.

I'm adding a fifth model to the ensemble that works at the node level. For each ROI on CC200, AAL and HO it uses global connectivity strength: the mean signed and mean absolute Fisher-z correlation with all other ROIs (weighted degree, or global brain connectivity). ADHD findings are mostly network-wide, such as weaker default-mode coherence and changed fronto-striatal hubness. These ~850 per-ROI summaries average out edge noise, so they should be a stronger signal in this setting with far more features than subjects, and bring information the edge-level tangent models don't capture.

I'm adding a sixth ensemble block of per-ROI dynamic-connectivity features, pooled across CC200, AAL and HO. Each ROI gets two values from sliding windows of 30 timepoints with a step of 3. The first is temporal variability (Zhang et al. 2016): 1 minus the mean correlation of the ROI's whole-brain connectivity profile between windows. The second is the SD of its windowed node strength. ADHD is linked to unstable network dynamics, such as fluctuating default-mode/task-positive anticorrelation, which the static covariance and strength blocks average away. The existing per-site standardization should remove the offset caused by TR and scan-length differences between sites.

Instead of one shared tangent-space reference point, each site's Ledoit-Wolf covariances are re-centred on that site's own log-Euclidean mean (Riemannian re-centring / parallel transport, as in Ng et al. 2016 and Zanini et al. 2018). Per-feature site z-scoring only removes per-edge shifts and scales. Re-centring per site also removes the site-specific congruence (mixing) of the whole covariance structure that comes from scanner and protocol differences. The three tangent blocks are the strongest part of the ensemble, so this should give them cleaner, better-aligned features across sites. The step uses no labels: it relies only on site metadata, and if site metadata can't be matched to the subjects, or a site has fewer than 8 subjects, it falls back to the global reference.

This adds a seventh ensemble block of network-level connectivity summaries. For each atlas, ROIs are grouped into data-driven modules at two scales (k=7 and k=17, in the spirit of Yeo's 7/17 networks). The grouping comes from KMeans on each ROI's group-mean Fisher-z connectivity profile, which uses no labels. Each subject's within- and between-module mean connectivity then becomes a feature, pooled across CC200, AAL and HO. ADHD findings are mostly at the network level, such as weaker default-mode coherence and changed default-mode/task-positive anticorrelation. These few hundred module summaries average out edge noise much more than the edge-level tangent features or the ROI-level strength features, so they should add a denoised, complementary signal in this setting with far more features than subjects.

This adds an eighth ensemble block of about 36 whole-brain features, 12 per atlas, pooled across CC200, AAL and HO. They cover global-signal amplitude, the share of variance it explains, and its autocorrelation and kurtosis, which track vigilance and arousal. They also cover DVARS level, spikiness and the fraction of spike frames, which pick up residual head motion. The last three describe the effective dimensionality of the ROI correlation spectrum. Children with ADHD move more and show more vigilance fluctuation and more global co-fluctuation in rs-fMRI. None of the existing per-edge, per-ROI or per-module blocks measures these properties of the whole scan.

Right now the eight block models are combined with a plain average of their raw decision scores. That gives every block the same weight, whatever its signal, and blocks whose scores have a larger scale count for more. This change estimates per-block weights by grouped inner CV on the training fold (using `groups_train`). Each block's out-of-fold scores are z-scored, and a logistic stacker is fitted on them. Negative weights are clipped to zero and the result is blended 50/50 with equal weights, so the weighting stays stable with about 700 subjects.

I'm adding a ninth ensemble block of partial-correlation features (Fisher-z), pooled across CC200, AAL and HO. They come from the inverse of the Ledoit-Wolf covariances the tangent blocks already compute. In the Dadi et al. 2019 benchmark on ADHD-200, partial correlation came second only to tangent-space. It measures direct links between ROIs, after accounting for every other ROI. That is different from the tangent and Pearson blocks, which mix direct and indirect coupling. So it should add complementary connectivity evidence for very little extra compute. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

ADHD-200 sites recruited children differently, so the share of boys and girls with ADHD differs from site to site. Separate site and sex effects can't represent that. I'm adding site×sex interaction columns at a moderate scale (effective ×5 instead of ×30), so each cell's base rate is partly shrunk toward the main effects rather than fit freely. This is shared by all eight block models.
